notes: 21.5, p. 526 specifies System.StackOverflowException for stack exhaustion. The pinned hosted .NET runtime terminates the process without entering the matching handler (STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW). This is a runtime departure; the program remains useful for targets that raise the specified exception.

Confirmed hosted-runtime departure under the exception-discard requirement, not an independently established base-call omission. The ancestor writes and flushes ANCESTOR before the expected OK 2; observed stdout is "ANCESTOR\n". The marker proves the base destructor ran. Process termination defeats exception discard, continuation and final counted output. The typed-catch repair emits both lines. No base-call departure is asserted.

23.3 (PDF p. 322, lines 14-17) says that if an exception escapes a destructor and there is no base class or no base class destructor, the exception is discarded; Container's only base is object, which has no C# destructor (17.12, PDF p. 282, lines 6-7 and 52), and which in any case has no base class. With the exception discarded, Main continues and prints OK 2. The typed-catch witness prints OK 2 on the same host, so the GC request and wait do run the destructor there (scheduling that 10.9, PDF p. 100, lines 2-7, leaves to the implementation), and the only remaining cause of failure is the undiscarded exception. The 7th edition's 21.4 (PDF p. 554) makes this behavior unspecified. Positive witnesses establish prerequisites; failing originals do not prove mutation sensitivity.
